title: GPT vs Opus: Where GPT-6.1 Sol Has the Edge
audience: AI tool users, developers, and technology-curious viewers comparing frontier models
thesis: GPT-6.1 Sol has a defensible edge in standard token prices and selected vendor-reported workflow costs, but it is not a universal winner over Claude Opus 5.5.
payoff: The useful winner is the model that solves your own tasks with the best measured balance of quality, time, and total cost.

visual_system.name: Interface Theatre
visual_system.signature_motif: A restrained comparison console uses paired model cards, task labels, highlighted metric strips, and focus rings to reveal one measurement at a time.
visual_system.palette_logic: Deep navy is the neutral workspace, teal marks GPT-6.1 Sol evidence, violet marks Claude Opus evidence, amber flags caveats, and white marks the shared conclusion.
visual_system.typography: Use a compact high-contrast sans serif; large numerals carry the metric while medium labels clarify model, unit, effort setting, and source.
visual_system.composition_grammar: Alternate paired comparison cards, a single delta panel, a proportional cost chart, and a counterexample benchmark table; reserve the most negative space for the verdict.
visual_system.motion_grammar: Focus rings activate the relevant panel, meters grow from zero to stated values, and small source labels persist; never animate unstated scores or suggest real-time live benchmark data.
avoid: Do not imply a vendor-reported benchmark is independently audited.
Do not use absolute scores where the source provides only a difference.
Do not equate low task cost with higher answer quality.
Do not state that one model wins every task or benchmark.

chapters.purpose: Open with the broad model question and narrow it to measurable advantages rather than a universal ranking.
Show standard input and output token prices on a like-for-like per-million-token basis.
Present selected workflow evidence with clear vendor attribution, effort settings, units, and caveats.
Show a credible coding benchmark where Opus 5.5 leads a reported GPT model, limiting the claim.
Deliver the defensible takeaway and tell viewers how to compare models on their own real tasks.

claims.text: GPT-6.1 Sol standard API rates are 2 dollars input and 10 dollars output per million tokens, within the listed standard pricing tier.
Claude Opus 5.5 lists standard API rates of 4 dollars input and 20 dollars output per million tokens.
OpenAI reports GPT-6.1 Sol 2.2 percentage points above Opus 5.5 on AutomationBench at medium reasoning and around one-third of the task cost.
OpenAI reports maximum-effort Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 average task costs of 5.47 dollars for GPT-6.1 Sol and 23.21 dollars for Opus 5.5.
Anthropic reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 scores of 66.4 percent for Opus 5.5 and 57.9 percent for GPT-6 Astra with different effort settings.
The cited results support task-specific trade-offs, not a universal ranking across every model task and production workflow.

scenes.viewer_question: What does it actually mean to say GPT is better than Opus?
scenes.visual_argument: A paired interface makes the comparison look concrete before the narration narrows the claim to selected measurable trade-offs.
scenes.visible_action: Two labeled model panels slide into a shared comparison workspace and reveal their model names without a winner badge.
scenes.topic_specificity: The panels name GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 so the claim is about concrete releases rather than vague model families.
scenes.composition: Use a large split headline above equal-width model cards with equal visual weight; keep the qualifier directly below the headline.
scenes.change_from_previous: This is the opening image; it establishes the two-model question rather than recycling another data chart.
scenes.motion_purpose: A measured entrance creates focus on the question while delaying any metric until the viewer knows the comparison.
scenes.hold_reason: Hold both model names and the qualifier long enough to read before shifting to listed rates.

scenes.viewer_question: Is the listed token price materially different before a task even starts?
scenes.visual_argument: The published standard input and output rates are half as high for GPT-6.1 Sol as for Opus 5.5.
scenes.visible_action: A two-column rate card displays input and output prices with proportional horizontal bars and an explicit per-million-token unit.
scenes.topic_specificity: The exact model identifiers and separate input/output rows prevent generic pricing claims and avoid confusing output costs with total task costs.
scenes.composition: Use balanced side-by-side model cards; align every price on the same row, put the dollar amount at the right edge, and reserve teal and violet for the two models.
scenes.change_from_previous: Move from a broad title and two hero panels to a compact rate table whose aligned rows enable direct comparison.
scenes.motion_purpose: Bars extend to their proportional listed values so viewers can compare rates at a glance without reading a dense table.
scenes.hold_reason: Keep the per-million-token unit and the note about caching and special modes visible while the 50-percent takeaway lands.

scenes.viewer_question: Does the lower listed price show up in any measured workflow result?
scenes.visual_argument: One OpenAI-reported AutomationBench comparison describes a small measured score lead alongside a substantially lower task cost.
scenes.visible_action: A delta panel reveals plus 2.2 percentage points, then a separate cost bar indicates roughly one-third of the reported task cost.
scenes.topic_specificity: The scene names AutomationBench, medium reasoning effort, and OpenAI as the reporting source so the figure is not passed off as an absolute universal score.
scenes.composition: Place the percentage-point delta in a large left panel and a separate paired cost meter on the right; keep attribution and the fallback/setup caveat beneath the meters.
scenes.change_from_previous: Replace exact token-price rows with a task-level result and separate score change from cost, preventing the viewer from treating the metrics as interchangeable.
scenes.motion_purpose: Reveal the score margin first and cost relationship second; sequencing shows that a performance metric and an expense metric answer different questions.
scenes.hold_reason: Hold the vendor attribution, benchmark name, and medium-effort setting together with the two metrics.

scenes.viewer_question: How far apart can the reported costs get on a scientific workflow?
scenes.visual_argument: The reported maximum-effort task-cost figures differ by more than four times, which highlights a cost-efficiency advantage but does not itself rank quality.
scenes.visible_action: Two vertical bars grow from a common baseline to 5.47 dollars and 23.21 dollars, with a calculated lower-cost callout and benchmark/mode labels.
scenes.topic_specificity: The scene names Terminal-Bench Science 0.1, maximum effort, and average cost per task; it never invents an undisclosed score.
scenes.composition: Give the chart the larger right portion of the frame, keep cost figures above bars, and place the 76-percent calculation and quality caveat in a left information rail.
scenes.change_from_previous: Move from a split score-and-cost panel to a single-unit vertical chart so the cost gap can be seen without suggesting a new benchmark score.
scenes.motion_purpose: Bars rise from the same baseline in proportion to reported costs; the movement communicates scale rather than drama.
scenes.hold_reason: Keep both exact amounts and the maximum-effort label visible long enough for comparison, with the cost-is-not-quality caveat remaining on screen.

scenes.viewer_question: What would disprove the claim that GPT wins everything?
scenes.visual_argument: A reported Terminal-Bench 4.0 comparison goes the other way: Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than GPT-6 Astra.
scenes.visible_action: The two published percentages animate into a pair of bars and a caveat card identifies Opus xhigh effort and GPT Astra high effort.
scenes.topic_specificity: The GPT model is explicitly labeled GPT-6 Astra, not GPT-6.1 Sol, and the effort mismatch is made visible so this counterexample cannot be misread as the same comparison as the preceding cost results.
scenes.composition: Keep the benchmark comparison in the broad left panel and a narrow right rail labeled what this means; use small but readable effort-setting notes beneath the percentages.
scenes.change_from_previous: Shift the visual emphasis from GPT's selected cost advantage to an Opus-led coding benchmark, changing both the metric and the model pairing.
scenes.motion_purpose: Both bars reveal their published percentages at the same pace, then the caveat gains a focus border to signal the limits of the comparison.
scenes.hold_reason: Hold the exact scores, source and different-effort note together so the counterexample is not separated from its qualification.

scenes.viewer_question: What should a viewer conclude and do with this comparison?
scenes.visual_argument: GPT-6.1 Sol has a concrete value case on listed rates and selected task-cost reports, while Opus remains competitive and leads the cited Terminal-Bench 4.0 comparison.
scenes.visible_action: Two closing model cards summarize the distinct strengths, then a single recommendation states to test both against quality, time and total cost on the user's own workload.
scenes.topic_specificity: The verdict reconnects the exact pricing and benchmark evidence while retaining the coding counterexample instead of repeating an unqualified headline.
scenes.composition: Return to two balanced cards, then place the test-your-own-workload rule in one full-width lower strip and the source URLs along the bottom edge.
scenes.change_from_previous: Recompose the benchmark detail into a balanced conclusion with a practical decision rule instead of presenting one more score.
scenes.motion_purpose: The two summaries enter in sequence and resolve into one steady rule; no new numbers appear during the closing beat.
scenes.hold_reason: Hold the conclusion and the two primary source URLs for several seconds so viewers can retain the takeaway and find the source ledger.
